prose_changes.old: The Rome Gregory was born into around 540 had been besieged, taken, retaken and emptied within living memory. The Gothic wars and Justinian's reconquest had wrecked the city and the countryside that fed it, and from 568 the Lombards held most of the peninsula. The imperial government sat at Ravenna and had little left to spend on Rome. Gregory was city prefect, gave it up, turned the family house on the Caelian into a monastery, and was sent to Constantinople as the pope's representative. He was elected bishop in 590, during a plague, and spent fourteen years doing a job that had quietly become something else. The letters show what it was. He ran the papal estates in Sicily as the city's food supply and audited the men who managed them. He paid soldiers and negotiated with Lombard dukes when the exarch would not. He ransomed prisoners. He told bishops in Gaul, Spain, Africa and Illyricum what he thought they were doing wrong, at length. He refused the title of universal bishop when Constantinople's patriarch used it, and called himself servant of the servants of God instead. And in 596 he sent a party of his own monks to Kent, and then wrote to them again and again about what to do with pagan temples and how far to insist on Roman custom. The Pastoral Rule, written at the beginning of it, is the book underneath all the rest: an argument that the government of souls is the art of arts, that different people must be told the same truth differently, and that wanting the office is itself a disqualification for it.

prose_changes.old: Irish monasticism reshaped continental Christianity: Columbanus's foundations seeded dozens of monasteries across Gaul and Italy, and Iona-trained missionaries carried the faith into Northumbria and beyond. The penitential handbooks written here spread through the Frankish church and stand behind the private, repeatable confession that became normal Western practice. Its scriptoria produced the insular manuscript style that culminates in the Book of Kells, and the high crosses and round towers of Irish monastic sites are among the most recognizable Christian monuments anywhere. Iona, Clonmacnoise and Glendalough are all still visited, and Iona has a working religious community again.

Irish scribes made the insular style of manuscript, which reaches its height in the Book of Kells. The high crosses and round towers of Irish monastic sites rank among the best-known Christian landmarks in the world. People still come to Iona, Clonmacnoise and Glendalough, and on Iona a religious community lives and works once more.

And Brittany, settled from Britain in these centuries, kept both a Celtic language and a cluster of British saints' cults that are still there.

prose_changes.old: The Visigoths ruled Spain as Homoian Christians for over a century, in uneasy coexistence with the Nicene population they governed — until King Reccared announced his own conversion and, at the third council of Toledo in 589, brought the Gothic bishops with him. Nothing quite like it happened anywhere else: a kingdom's own church council formally abandoned its creed and adopted its subjects'. What followed was one of the more remarkable intellectual efforts of the early Middle Ages. Isidore of Seville set out to gather what survived of classical learning into a single encyclopedia, and his circle — his brother Leander, Braulio of Zaragoza, Ildefonsus of Toledo — produced letters, liturgy, histories and rules around him. The councils of Toledo worked as something between a synod and a parliament, legislating for church and kingdom together, and their record also includes a harsh and escalating body of law against Spain's Jews. All of it ended abruptly with the Muslim conquest of 711.

prose_changes.old: Ireland was never Roman, and the church that took root there in the fifth century organized itself accordingly — around monasteries and their abbots rather than around city bishops, with monastic families and founder-saints anchoring whole regions. Patrick's two short surviving letters, a defense of his own life and a furious protest at the enslavement of his converts, are the only certainly authentic voices from the beginning, and they are startlingly personal. Two things it produced were absorbed by the wider church. Peregrinatio, the practice of leaving home permanently for God's sake, which sent Columba to Iona in 563 and Columbanus into Gaul and Italy, where he founded Luxeuil and Bobbio and argued with Frankish kings. And the penitentials, handbooks assigning particular penances to particular sins, which quietly turned confession into something private and repeatable. Its own way of calculating Easter and its distinctive tonsure eventually collided with Roman practice, and at Whitby in 664 the Northumbrian king ruled against the Irish reckoning.

The other was the penitentials, handbooks that set out the penance for each kind of sin. Its own way of reckoning Easter, and its own style of tonsure, in time clashed with Roman practice. At Whitby in 664 the Northumbrian king ruled against the Irish reckoning.

Its Indian branch, the St Thomas Christians of Kerala, is the ancestor of several churches worshipping there today, and its heirs survive as the Assyrian Church of the East and the Chaldean Catholic Church. Along the way its scholars translated Greek medicine, philosophy and logic into Syriac, work later carried on into Arabic — one of the routes by which Greek learning reached the wider medieval world.
